subtopics: Writing Maintainable Code and Useful Documentation
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main behavior of writing maintainable code and useful documentation.

content.intro: This lesson introduces writing maintainable code and useful documentation as part of testing, debugging, and code quality. It turns the curriculum heading into a short, practical concept guide with a visual, example, and checks to try locally.
content.why_it_matters: Writing Maintainable Code and Useful Documentation belongs to Testing, Debugging, and Code Quality. Focus on the specific rule it introduces, compare one correct example with a nearby edge case, and explain the difference in your own words.

content_blocks.title: How to work with it
content_blocks.text: For writing maintainable code and useful documentation, identify the inputs and assumptions first. Use the smallest useful example, predict its behavior, run it in a local Python interpreter, and compare the observed result with your prediction. The example below is a static reference in CodeLeaf, not executed Python.

content_blocks.title: Version and reliability note
content_blocks.text: Use the interpreter and dependencies declared for your project. Where a feature is version-specific or tool-dependent, check its official documentation and document a useful fallback.

content.task: Try it yourself: adapt the example to demonstrate writing maintainable code and useful documentation with different inputs. Write down your prediction, run it locally, and explain the result plus one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the central idea in writing maintainable code and useful documentation without copying the definition.
Run or manually verify the smallest example using the stated runtime assumptions.
Describe one relevant edge case, limitation, or troubleshooting step.
hints: Read the sample carefully and identify the values or state that affect the result.
Change one variable or input at a time and predict what should happen before running it.
Check the official reference and runtime version if behavior differs from the expected result.
